questions.q: The Wittig reaction converts an aldehyde or ketone into:
c: An alkene, using a phosphonium ylide
questions.e: The ylide's carbon replaces the carbonyl oxygen; Ph₃P=O is the by-product.

questions.q: Compared with non-stabilized ylides, stabilized ylides (with an adjacent EWG such as an ester) typically give:
questions.e: Reversible betaine/oxaphosphetane formation leads to the thermodynamically favored E-alkene; non-stabilized ylides give Z.

questions.q: A key advantage of the Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons reaction is:
c: E-selective α,β-unsaturated ester formation and water-soluble phosphate by-product
questions.e: Phosphonate carbanions are more nucleophilic than stabilized ylides, and the dialkyl phosphate by-product is removed by aqueous workup.

questions.q: The Reformatsky reaction uses:
c: An α-halo ester with zinc to add to a carbonyl
An α-halo ketone with Mg to make an alkene
A vinyl boronic acid with Pd
questions.e: The organozinc enolate adds to aldehydes/ketones to give β-hydroxy esters.

questions.q: The Claisen rearrangement of an allyl vinyl ether gives:
c: A γ,δ-unsaturated carbonyl via a [3,3]-sigmatropic shift
questions.e: A chair-like six-membered TS forms a C–C bond while breaking the C–O bond.

questions.q: The Cope rearrangement is a:
questions.e: 1,5-Dienes isomerize via a chair-like six-center TS, equilibrating to the more stable diene.

questions.q: Heating allyl phenyl ether gives mostly:
questions.e: [3,3] shift to the ortho carbon, followed by tautomerization (rearomatization) to the phenol.

questions.q: The Beckmann rearrangement converts cyclohexanone oxime (acid) into:
questions.e: The group anti to the leaving group on N migrates, forming a ring-expanded amide.

questions.q: In Baeyer–Villiger oxidation, the group with the highest migratory aptitude among those listed is:
questions.e: Approximate order: tert-alkyl > cyclohexyl > sec-alkyl ≈ benzyl > phenyl > primary alkyl > methyl.

questions.q: The Hofmann rearrangement of a primary amide (Br₂, NaOH) gives:
c: A primary amine with one fewer carbon
An amine with one more carbon
questions.e: Via an N-bromoamide, isocyanate and decarboxylation.

questions.q: The Curtius rearrangement converts an acyl azide into an isocyanate with loss of:
questions.e: Thermal rearrangement with retention of configuration at the migrating carbon.

questions.q: The Sonogashira coupling forms a C–C bond between:
c: A terminal alkyne and an aryl/vinyl halide, using Pd and Cu(I)
questions.e: Pd and a Cu co-catalyst with an amine base form the enyne or arylalkyne.

questions.q: Which pairing of reaction name and organometallic partner is correct?
questions.e: Suzuki uses boron, Stille tin, Negishi zinc, Kumada magnesium (Grignard).

questions.q: The Buchwald–Hartwig reaction forms:
c: C–N bonds (aryl amines) from aryl halides and amines
questions.e: Pd, a bulky phosphine ligand and a base.

questions.q: The Wolff–Kishner reduction converts C=O to CH₂ under:
c: Strongly basic conditions with hydrazine at high temperature
questions.e: Clemmensen uses Zn(Hg)/HCl (acidic); choose between them by substrate sensitivity.

questions.q: The Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation uses:
c: Ti(OiPr)₄, a tartrate ester and t-BuOOH on allylic alcohols
OsO₄ and NMO on any alkene
questions.e: The allylic OH binds Ti; the chiral tartrate directs the face of epoxidation.

questions.q: The Birch reduction of benzene (Na, NH₃(l), ROH) gives:
questions.e: Electron addition, protonation and a second electron/proton sequence leave a non-conjugated 1,4-diene.

questions.q: The Mitsunobu reaction of a chiral secondary alcohol with a carboxylic acid (PPh₃, DEAD) gives an ester with:
questions.e: The alcohol is activated as an oxyphosphonium; the carboxylate displaces by SN2.

questions.q: The Williamson ether synthesis is best performed with:
c: An alkoxide and a primary alkyl halide
An alkoxide and a tertiary alkyl halide

questions.q: Why does the Mitsunobu reaction proceed with inversion, and what limits the nucleophile choice?
questions.m: PPh₃ and the azodicarboxylate form a betaine that activates the alcohol as an alkoxyphosphonium (excellent leaving group). The conjugate base of the pronucleophile then attacks the carbon in an SN2 fashion, giving inversion. The nucleophile must be acidic enough (pKa ≲ 11–13) to protonate the betaine; very weakly acidic nucleophiles fail or give hydrazide by-products.
